chunks.text: 2.1 Pathology foundation models and MIL Pathology foundation models (PFMs) encode hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained histopathology images into general-purpose embeddings that support a wide range of downstream tasks ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2024 ; Filiot et al., 2025 ; Vorontsov et al., 2024 ) . These representations are learned through large-scale pretraining, using objectives such as self-supervision ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Vorontsov et al., 2024 ) and vision-language contrastive learning ( Lu et al., 2024 ) . In pathology practice, inference is performed on whole-slide images (WSIs), which often reach gigapixel scale (e.g., 100,000 × 100,000 100{,}000\times 100{,}000 pixels). The predominant pipeline therefore segments the WSI, divides it into patches, encodes the patches independently using a PFM, and then aggregates the patch embeddings into a slide-level embedding using a multiple instance learning (MIL) module ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . MIL addresses learning from bags of instances for which supervision is available only at the bag level ( Dietterich et al., 1997 ) . In digital pathology, a WSI is treated as a bag of patches ( Campanella et al., 2019 ) : while a WSI-level label may indicate, for example, the presence of cancer, labels for the individual patches are generally unavailable. MIL methods therefore aggregate patch embeddings into a single slide-level representation from which the downstream task can be predicted. A wide range of MIL methods have been proposed, varying along several dimensions, such as their aggregation mechanisms, architectures, and whether the aggregation is learnable or parameter-free. An influential architecture is ABMIL ( Ilse et al., 2018 ) , which learns a network that assigns attention weights to instances and aggregates them through a weighted average. Subsequent methods introduce more sophisticated aggregation mechanisms.

For example, DSMIL ( Li et al., 2021 ) identifies a critical instance and uses it to guide attention over the remaining instances, while TransMIL ( Shao et al., 2021 ) employs transformer-based attention to model dependencies between patches. A common practice is to train MIL models from scratch for each downstream task, while more recent work has explored pretraining slide-level MIL models ( Ding et al., 2025 ; Shao et al., 2025 ) . 3 Method 3.1 Problem setup and domain adaptation for MIL (a) (b) Figure 2: Analysis of the interaction between domain adaptation and ABMIL aggregation. (a) Standard UDA (single-stage) concentrates attention on a smaller subset of patches than source-only training. AdaptMIL reduces and even reverses this effect, resulting in a more distributed attention pattern. In UDA, we are given n s n_{s} labeled samples from a source domain { ( x i s , y i s ) } i = 1 n s \{(x_{i}^{s},y_{i}^{s})\}_{i=1}^{n_{s}} , together with n t n_{t} unlabeled samples from a target domain, { x j t } j = 1 n t \{x_{j}^{t}\}_{j=1}^{n_{t}} . In the cross-hospital setting, each sample x x is a WSI, the labels y i y_{i} correspond to biological classes (e.g., cancer status), and each domain corresponds to a different hospital. The goal is to learn a MIL module and a task head (e.g., a classifier) that generalize to the target hospital without having access to its labels. Domain-invariant UDA methods jointly optimize a supervised task loss on labeled source samples and a domain adaptation objective that encourages alignment between source and target representations ( Wilson and Cook, 2020 ) .

(a) (b) Figure 3: AdaptMIL two-stage training with ABMIL for classification. (a) In Stage 1, a projection layer is trained to map patch embeddings into a more domain-aligned space. The projected embeddings are aggregated using mean pooling, and training uses both a cross-entropy (CE) loss on labeled source slides and a domain adaptation (DA) loss between source and target slide embeddings. (b) In Stage 2, mean pooling is replaced by ABMIL’s learnable attention module. The projection layer is frozen, and the attention module and classifier are trained using only labeled source slides. As in standard domain-invariant UDA, the feature extractor (the PFM) can remain frozen while a learnable projection transforms its representations into a more domain-aligned space. In many MIL architectures such a projection is already included prior to aggregation ( Shao et al., 2021 ; Ilse et al., 2018 ; Lu et al., 2021 ) , eliminating the need for an additional projection layer. The MIL module and task head are thus trained jointly, with the only difference from standard source-only MIL training (using only labeled source data and the task loss) being the addition of the domain adaptation loss. 3.2 Failure mode of domain adaptation and MIL training We find that the application of UDA to MIL training ( Eq. 2 ) is mostly ineffective, performing worse than source-only training in most settings and providing only limited gains otherwise (see Fig.

1 ). Analyzing this reveals a surprising effect: joint MIL and domain adaptation training substantially changes the learned attention pattern compared to standard MIL training, concentrating attention on a smaller subset of patches. We demonstrate this effect in Fig. 2(a) : Under UDA training, the top- k k attended patches in ABMIL account for a substantially larger fraction of the total attention (e.g., 2.8 × 2.8\times for k = 50 k=50 ). This shows that the adaptation objective affects not only the learned projection layer, as might be expected, but also how patch information is aggregated by the MIL module. Examining the training dynamics shows that both the task and domain adaptation losses decrease as expected ( Fig. 2(b) ), indicating that the optimization objectives are satisfied. Together with the degradation in performance, this suggests that the MIL model takes advantage of a shortcut to reduce the domain gap. That is, rather than learning genuinely more domain-robust representations, it can satisfy both objectives by changing how patch information is aggregated. We hypothesize that this shortcut is facilitated by the morphological redundancy across patches in WSIs ( Song et al., 2024 ) , which may provide the MIL model with multiple ways to satisfy the task objective. Adding the domain adaptation constraint may therefore push the model toward a different aggregation solution that, in this case, generalizes worse. We emphasize that more concentrated attention is not inherently undesirable, as its effect depends on the regions receiving high attention and the quality of the representations. Our analysis therefore does not imply that concentrated attention alone causes performance degradation. Rather, it shows that domain adaptation can substantially alter the learned aggregation pattern, even though the intended effect is to only make representations more domain-invariant, and that these changes are associated with degraded performance.

3.3 AdaptMIL Our analysis shows that applying domain adaptation objectives interferes with MIL aggregation learning. This motivated us to try and decouple the two, namely separate domain-invariant representation learning from learning the aggregation mechanism. We propose AdaptMIL , a two-stage training strategy that first learns domain-aligned representations and then learns the MIL aggregation over the adapted representations. AdaptMIL is formulated here using ABMIL ( Ilse et al., 2018 ) but can be applied to different MIL architectures. See Fig. 3 for an illustration of AdaptMIL. ABMIL first transforms each patch representation through a learned projection layer P P , and then aggregates the projected representations with an attention module Attn \mathrm{Attn} . Let z i , k = f PFM ​ ( p i , k ) z_{i,k}=f_{\mathrm{PFM}}(p_{i,k}) denote the representation of patch k k from slide i i . ABMIL is given by h MIL ​ ( z i ) = Attn ⁡ ( P ⁡ ( z i ) ) h_{\mathrm{MIL}}(z_{i})=\mathrm{Attn}\!\left(P(z_{i})\right) , where P P is applied independently to each patch representation, i.e., P ⁡ ( z i ) = { P ⁡ ( z i , 1 ) , … , P ⁡ ( z i , m i ) } P(z_{i})=\{P(z_{i,1}),\ldots,P(z_{i,m_{i}})\} . In the first stage, AdaptMIL learns a projection layer P P that maps patch representations into a more domain-invariant space, and does not use the attention module. To obtain slide-level representations for the task and domain alignment objectives without the attention module, the projected representations are aggregated using parameter-free mean pooling.

The resulting Stage 1 objective is: ℒ stage1 = 1 n s ​ ∑ i = 1 n s ℒ task ​ ( g ϕ ​ ( f mean ​ ( P ⁡ ( z i s ) ) ) , y i s ) + λ ​ ℒ DA ​ ( { f mean ​ ( P ⁡ ( z i s ) ) } i = 1 n s , { f mean ​ ( P ⁡ ( z j t ) ) } j = 1 n t ) , \begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{stage1}}&=\frac{1}{n_{s}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{s}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{task}}\!\left(g_{\phi}\!\left(f_{\mathrm{mean}}(P(z_{i}^{s}))\right),\,y_{i}^{s}\right)\\ &\quad+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DA}}\!\left(\{f_{\mathrm{mean}}(P(z_{i}^{s}))\}_{i=1}^{n_{s}},\{f_{\mathrm{mean}}(P(z_{j}^{t}))\}_{j=1}^{n_{t}}\right),\end{split} (3) where f mean ​ ( P ⁡ ( z i ) ) = 1 m i ​ ∑ k = 1 m i P ⁡ ( z i , k ) f_{\mathrm{mean}}(P(z_{i}))=\frac{1}{m_{i}}\sum_{k=1}^{m_{i}}P(z_{i,k}) . Mean pooling is a simple but competitive aggregation strategy in computational pathology ( Shao et al., 2025 ) . Importantly, because it is parameter-free, it cannot be altered by the domain adaptation objective. In the second stage, AdaptMIL learns the MIL aggregation over the adapted representations. It keeps the projection layer P P learned in Stage 1 frozen and replaces mean pooling with ABMIL’s attention module, recovering the full ABMIL architecture. We train this stage using only source samples and the task loss. This allows the learnable attention module to focus on task-discriminative information without being influenced by the domain adaptation objective. The resulting Stage 2 objective is: ℒ stage2 = 1 n s ​ ∑ i = 1 n s ℒ task ​ ( g ϕ ​ ( h MIL ​ ( z i s ) ) , y i s ) . \begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{stage2}}&=\frac{1}{n_{s}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{s}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{task}}\!\left(g_{\phi}\!\left(h_{\mathrm{MIL}}(z_{i}^{s})\right),\,y_{i}^{s}\right).\end{split} (4) As shown in Fig. 1 , the decoupled two-stage training of AdaptMIL improves over both source-only training and standard UDA. 2(a) shows that AdaptMIL does not exhibit the increased attention concentration observed with standard UDA and instead produces more distributed attention. 4 Experiments 4.1 Tasks and datasets We evaluate AdaptMIL on four different tasks. The first is non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) subtyping between lung adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, using 489 WSIs from TCGA ( Komura et al., 2022 ) across six hospitals, and 150 WSIs from an in-house hospital dataset. The second task is renal cell carcinoma (RCC) subtyping between clear cell carcinoma and papillary cell carcinoma, using 307 WSIs from TCGA across three hospitals. The third task is cancer detection, using 404 WSIs from CAMELYON17 ( Bandi et al., 2018 ) across five hospitals. The fourth task is survival prediction, presented in Sec. D.3 of the supplementary material (Supp.). 4.2 Evaluation For each subtyping or detection dataset, we evaluate all source-target hospital pairs and report the average metric across them. For example, the TCGA NSCLC dataset contains six hospitals, resulting in 30 source-target pairs. For the in-house lung dataset, we evaluate both directions with each of the six TCGA hospitals, resulting in 12 pairs. Each source-target pair is evaluated using 3-fold cross-validation, with evaluation performed on held-out target WSIs that are not used during training. Our main metric for subtyping and detection is balanced accuracy. Table 1: Cross-hospital NSCLC TCGA subtyping results for AdaptMIL with ABMIL. The metric is balanced accuracy (%). For patch-level feature extraction, we use three PFMs: UNI ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , CONCH-1.5 ( Lu et al., 2024 ) , and H0-mini ( Filiot et al., 2025 ) . Tissue segmentation, patch extraction, and feature extraction are performed using the TRIDENT package ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . We evaluate four domain adaptation objectives: three discrepancy-based losses, MMD ( Long et al., 2015 ) , LMMD ( Zhu et al., 2020 ) , and CORAL ( Sun and Saenko, 2016 ) , and the adversarial DANN objective ( Ganin et al., 2016 ) . We further apply AdaptMIL to three MIL architectures: ABMIL ( Ilse et al., 2018 ) , DSMIL ( Li et al., 2021 ) , and TITAN ( Ding et al., 2025 ) . The implementation for ABMIL is described in Sec. 3.3 . The implementations for DSMIL and TITAN follow the same principle with architecture-specific adjustments. All AdaptMIL models are trained for 80 epochs, with 40 epochs for each stage. Further implementation details are provided in Appendix A of the Supp. 4.4 Method comparisons We compare AdaptMIL against several baselines.

First, we compare against source-only training with standard MIL. This baseline, commonly referred to as empirical risk minimization (ERM) ( Vapnik, 1999 ) , represents the out-of-distribution performance that domain adaptation aims to improve. We also compare to standard UDA applied to MIL (defined in Eq. 2 ), using each of the four domain adaptation objectives. We refer to this baseline as single-stage UDA. We additionally compare against Macenko stain normalization ( Macenko et al., 2009 ) . In this setting, the MIL model is trained only on source data, as in ERM, but evaluation is performed on target images whose appearance is normalized to a source reference. Finally, we compare against a domain adaptation approach that fine-tunes the PFM using patch-level supervision ( Vardi et al., 2026 ) . We note that, to the best of our knowledge, other pathology-specific domain adaptation methods do not have publicly available implementations, and therefore we could not compare against them. 1 presents the evaluation of AdaptMIL with ABMIL across different PFMs and domain adaptation objectives on the NSCLC subtyping task. AdaptMIL improves over ERM across all PFMs and objectives, with gains up to + 6.02 % +6.02\% in balanced accuracy. MMD is the best-performing objective for two of the three PFMs, while LMMD and CORAL also yield notable gains, and DANN provides smaller improvements. Similar trends are observed for ROC-AUC and F1 (see Tab. 6(b) in Supp.). We additionally report in-domain performance of an ABMIL model that is trained and evaluated on samples from the same hospital. The performance drop from in-domain to source-only ERM highlights the degradation caused by the cross-hospital distribution shift. AdaptMIL substantially reduces this gap. As observed in Sec. 3.2 , directly applying standard single-stage UDA during MIL training often fails to improve over ERM and can substantially degrade performance. For example, LMMD with H0-mini reduces balanced accuracy by 20.24 % 20.24\% .

Macenko normalization also fails to improve performance, consistent with previous reports ( Huang et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2025 ) . Patch-level fine-tuning of PFMs is the baseline that provides the largest gains over ERM, but it remains inferior to AdaptMIL. Although effective, patch-level fine-tuning requires both patch supervision and re-extraction of patch features for every source–target adaptation setting. In contrast, AdaptMIL requires only slide-level supervision and operates on pre-extracted PFM features, allowing the same features to be reused across adaptation settings. We evaluate AdaptMIL across additional datasets and classification tasks in Tab. 2 . AdaptMIL improves over source-only ERM in eight of the nine settings, with gains of up to + 8.12 % +8.12\% . The only exception is cancer detection with CONCH-1.5, where ERM already achieves very strong performance. In contrast, single-stage UDA degrades performance in seven of the nine settings. Finally, we evaluate AdaptMIL with MIL architectures beyond ABMIL in Tab. 4 . AdaptMIL improves performance with DSMIL, although standard single-stage UDA is also effective. We further obtain a gain when adapting the pretrained TITAN slide encoder. These results indicate that AdaptMIL is not specific to ABMIL and can be applied to other MIL architectures. 4.6 Ablations We perform ablation studies to examine the impact of AdaptMIL’s components, with results for AdaptMIL-MMD with ABMIL and UNI in Tab. 4 . We first consider an alternative way to decouple representation alignment from aggregation learning. Instead of two-stage training, we train ABMIL throughout with the task objective, while applying the adaptation objective to a separate mean-pooling head placed after the projection layer. This prevents adaptation gradients from reaching the attention module, while still adapting the projection layer. This alternative method performs well (row 2 in Tab.

4 ), but remains inferior to AdaptMIL, suggesting an additional benefit from explicitly separating alignment and aggregation learning into distinct training stages. We next examine whether the second stage of AdaptMIL is necessary. Specifically, we use only Stage 1, where the learned projection is followed by mean pooling and trained with both the task and adaptation objectives. This performs worse than full AdaptMIL (row 3), confirming the benefit of using ABMIL, consistent with prior work favoring ABMIL over mean pooling ( Shao et al., 2025 ) . We additionally evaluate two design choices in Stage 2. Keeping the adaptation loss active in Stage 2 degrades performance (row 4), supporting our hypothesis that adaptation gradients interfere with aggregation learning. Not freezing the projection layer in Stage 2 slightly reduces performance (row 5), possibly because the projection becomes more source-oriented. Finally, we test whether the two-stage training schedule itself contributes to the improvement by removing the adaptation objective (row 6). This variant still improves over ERM, suggesting that separating representation and aggregation learning provides some benefit on its own. However, it remains substantially below AdaptMIL, demonstrating the importance of the alignment in Stage 1. 4.1 Tasks and datasets We evaluate AdaptMIL on four different tasks. As observed in Sec. 3.2 , directly applying standard single-stage UDA during MIL training often fails to improve over ERM and can substantially degrade performance. For example, LMMD with H0-mini reduces balanced accuracy by 20.24 % 20.24\% . Macenko normalization also fails to improve performance, consistent with previous reports ( Huang et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2025 ) . Patch-level fine-tuning of PFMs is the baseline that provides the largest gains over ERM, but it remains inferior to AdaptMIL. Although effective, patch-level fine-tuning requires both patch supervision and re-extraction of patch features for every source–target adaptation setting. In contrast, AdaptMIL requires only slide-level supervision and operates on pre-extracted PFM features, allowing the same features to be reused across adaptation settings. We evaluate AdaptMIL across additional datasets and classification tasks in Tab. 2 . AdaptMIL improves over source-only ERM in eight of the nine settings, with gains of up to + 8.12 % +8.12\% . The only exception is cancer detection with CONCH-1.5, where ERM already achieves very strong performance. In contrast, single-stage UDA degrades performance in seven of the nine settings. Finally, we evaluate AdaptMIL with MIL architectures beyond ABMIL in Tab. 4 . AdaptMIL improves performance with DSMIL, although standard single-stage UDA is also effective. We further obtain a gain when adapting the pretrained TITAN slide encoder. These results indicate that AdaptMIL is not specific to ABMIL and can be applied to other MIL architectures.

4.6 Ablations We perform ablation studies to examine the impact of AdaptMIL’s components, with results for AdaptMIL-MMD with ABMIL and UNI in Tab. 4 . We first consider an alternative way to decouple representation alignment from aggregation learning. Instead of two-stage training, we train ABMIL throughout with the task objective, while applying the adaptation objective to a separate mean-pooling head placed after the projection layer. This prevents adaptation gradients from reaching the attention module, while still adapting the projection layer. This alternative method performs well (row 2 in Tab. 4 ), but remains inferior to AdaptMIL, suggesting an additional benefit from explicitly separating alignment and aggregation learning into distinct training stages. We next examine whether the second stage of AdaptMIL is necessary. Specifically, we use only Stage 1, where the learned projection is followed by mean pooling and trained with both the task and adaptation objectives. This performs worse than full AdaptMIL (row 3), confirming the benefit of using ABMIL, consistent with prior work favoring ABMIL over mean pooling ( Shao et al., 2025 ) . We additionally evaluate two design choices in Stage 2. Keeping the adaptation loss active in Stage 2 degrades performance (row 4), supporting our hypothesis that adaptation gradients interfere with aggregation learning. Not freezing the projection layer in Stage 2 slightly reduces performance (row 5), possibly because the projection becomes more source-oriented. Finally, we test whether the two-stage training schedule itself contributes to the improvement by removing the adaptation objective (row 6). This variant still improves over ERM, suggesting that separating representation and aggregation learning provides some benefit on its own. However, it remains substantially below AdaptMIL, demonstrating the importance of the alignment in Stage 1.

5 Conclusion In this paper, we introduce AdaptMIL, a training strategy for performing domain adaptation within MIL architectures. Motivated by the observation that applying standard UDA to MIL can interfere with aggregation learning and degrade performance, AdaptMIL decouples domain alignment and aggregation learning into two training stages. Evaluated in cross-hospital adaptation settings with different tasks, PFMs, MIL architectures, and domain adaptation objectives, AdaptMIL consistently improves over source-only training and outperforms alternative adaptation methods. Our work has several limitations. We primarily evaluate MIL models trained from scratch, which is the most common setting and offers flexibility in the choice of the PFM ( Shao et al., 2025 ) . Another approach is to use pretrained MIL models, which avoid training from scratch but are tied to specific PFM features. Our TITAN experiments show that AdaptMIL can be applied in this setting, although broader evaluation remains for future work. A further limitation is that AdaptMIL depends on the quality of the PFM representations and may not be able to compensate for strong representation biases. Combining AdaptMIL with end-to-end PFM fine-tuning ( Kumar and Vanderbilt, 2026 ) is therefore an interesting direction for future work. Finally, our survival prediction results (in Supp.) show that AdaptMIL improves in this setting, while standard UDA can sometimes be effective, motivating further study of when decoupling domain alignment from MIL aggregation is necessary. We focus on cross-hospital domain adaptation in digital pathology, but AdaptMIL may also apply to other MIL settings affected by a domain shift. Examples include shifts between frozen and formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissues in pathology ( Ozyoruk et al., 2022 ) , as well as MIL applications in other domains such as medical imaging ( Cheplygina et al., 2019 ) and remote sensing ( Paheding et al., 2024 ) .

Across all 12 PFM and adaptation method combinations, single-stage UDA yields a higher average top-50 attention mass than ERM on held-out target slides, with the difference being statistically significant in 11 of the 12 settings.

Conversely, AdaptMIL produces a more distributed attention pattern than ERM in all 12 settings, with statistically significant differences in 11 of the 12 settings. We hypothesize that this occurs because Stage 1 learns the projection using mean pooling, which aggregates patch representations uniformly, and this affects the attention patterns subsequently learned in Stage 2. Lastly, for completeness, we show that the source cross-entropy and domain adaptation losses exhibit similar dynamics in single-stage UDA and AdaptMIL. Fig. 4 extends Fig. 2(b) by also showing the AdaptMIL losses, which follow a similar pattern. Despite the similar optimization behavior, single-stage UDA performs 3.21 % 3.21\% below ERM in this example, whereas AdaptMIL improves over ERM by 17.65 % 17.65\% , further supporting our hypothesis that single-stage UDA exploits a shortcut. D.3 Survival prediction In the main paper, we evaluate AdaptMIL on three classification tasks. Here, we additionally consider a non-classification task: survival prediction, which ranks patients according to their disease-specific survival risk. We use 312 patients from the TCGA kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC) cohort across three hospitals. Evaluation is performed using leave-one-out hospital evaluation with 5-fold cross-validation, and performance is measured using the concordance index (C-Index). Implementation uses the same ABMIL-based training framework, replacing the classification head and cross-entropy loss with a single-output risk head that predicts each patient’s log relative hazard. The model is trained with the negative Cox partial log-likelihood. Tab. 7 presents the survival prediction results.

AdaptMIL improves over ERM for all evaluated PFMs. However, unlike the classification tasks, single-stage UDA is also effective and even outperforms AdaptMIL, although the margins are mostly small. We observe an increase in attention concentration under single-stage UDA, as shown in Fig. 2(a) for NSCLC subtyping and in the other classification tasks. However, the increase in top-50 attention mass is much smaller for survival prediction. For example, with UNI and MMD it increases by only 1.2 × 1.2\times , compared with 2.8 × 2.8\times for NSCLC subtyping. This suggests that the interaction between domain adaptation and MIL aggregation may depend on the downstream task. Nevertheless, AdaptMIL still improves over source-only training across all evaluated PFMs, suggesting a more robust choice when the effectiveness of single-stage UDA is uncertain.
